source.quote: ### [Kubernetes Basics](kubernetes-basics/) — 8 modules

claims.rationale: The prerequisites hub (committed git object) names this section "Kubernetes Basics" and links it at kubernetes-basics/, so the page title is the established section name (astro.config.mjs, also a candidate, labels the autogenerated sidebar group "Kubernetes Basics" for directory prerequisites/kubernetes-basics).

source.quote: The practical Kubernetes starter path with `kubectl`, Pods, Deployments, Services, config, and YAML.

additional_sources.quote: **Prerequisites**: Docker installed, Cloud Native 101 completed
You will learn to explain containers, Docker images, what Kubernetes adds

claims.rationale: The hub describes the section as the practical Kubernetes starter path (concepts and practical skills); module 1.1 requires Docker and Cloud Native 101, and Cloud Native 101 teaches containers and Docker, so the audience is people who already know containers and now learn Kubernetes.

source.quote: This module teaches you to build that local arena, inspect its moving parts

additional_sources.quote: `kubectl` is the official Kubernetes command-line client
Essential commands to master.

claims.rationale: Module 1.1 is first and builds a local cluster; module 1.2 then teaches interacting with the cluster through kubectl, which module 1.1 calls the official Kubernetes command-line client. The sequence (cluster first, then kubectl) matches the sentence.

source.quote:
Kubernetes provides a command line tool for communicating with a Kubernetes cluster's
control plane,
using the Kubernetes API.
This tool is named kubectl.

claims.rationale: The Kubernetes reference page presents kubectl as the command line tool Kubernetes provides for communicating with the cluster. The word "standard" is not literal in the source; it is read as "the tool Kubernetes itself provides", which the quoted text states, and the page offers no other tool. Accepted on that reading.

source.quote: Pods are the smallest deployable units of computing that you can create and manage in Kubernetes.

claims.rationale: Source: Pods are the smallest deployable units that can be created and managed in Kubernetes. "Atomic units" is the page's figurative wording for the smallest-deployable-unit property (also the module 1.3 title), not an extra technical claim.

source.quote: DESIRED displays the desired number of replicas of the application, which you define when you create the Deployment. This is the desired state.

additional_sources.quote: Create a Deployment to rollout a ReplicaSet.
the Deployment Controller changes the actual state to the desired state at a controlled rate
Expose an application running in your cluster behind a single outward-facing endpoint, even when the workload is split across multiple backends.
that Deployment can create and destroy Pods dynamically

claims.rationale: Deployment page: the desired replica count is defined on the Deployment, the controller drives actual state to the desired state, and Deployments roll out new ReplicaSets. Service page: one endpoint fronts a set of Pods that a Deployment creates and destroys dynamically. Both halves of the sentence are covered; "stable endpoint" corresponds to the single endpoint that persists independent of which backends exist.

source.quote: Design** decoupled deployment architectures that move environment-specific settings out of container images and into ConfigMaps or Secrets.

additional_sources.quote: Namespaces divide the API into logical rooms, while labels attach structured identity to the objects inside those rooms.
it is the front door to the API server's declarative contract
persisted as desired state

claims.rationale: Module 1.6 moves configuration out of container images into ConfigMaps/Secrets; module 1.7 organizes resources with namespaces and labels; module 1.8 teaches YAML manifests as the declarative contract persisted as desired state. All three clauses are covered.

source.quote: A ConfigMap allows you to decouple environment-specific configuration from your container images, so that your applications are easily portable.

additional_sources.quote:
Such information might otherwise be put in a
Pod specification or in a
container image. Using a
Secret means that you don't need to include confidential data in your
application code.

claims.rationale: ConfigMap page states the decoupling of configuration from container images directly; Secret page states Secrets keep sensitive data out of Pod specs and container images. Together they support the whole claim.

source.quote:
Labels can be used to organize and to select subsets of
objects.

additional_sources.quote: namespaces provide a mechanism for isolating groups of resources within a single cluster

claims.rationale: Labels page: labels organize and select subsets of objects; Namespaces page: namespaces isolate groups of resources within a cluster. Both organize resources.

source.quote:
When you create an object in Kubernetes, you must provide the object spec that describes its
desired state

additional_sources.quote:
One way to create a Deployment using a manifest file like the one above is to use the
kubectl apply command
in the kubectl command-line interface, passing the .yaml file as an argument.

claims.rationale: Source: an object is described by a spec stating its desired state, supplied as a .yaml manifest applied with kubectl. Supports describing desired state using YAML manifests.

source.quote: Kubernetes Secrets are, by default, stored unencrypted in the API server's underlying data store

additional_sources.quote: In order to safely use Secrets, take at least the following steps:
Enable Encryption at Rest for Secrets.

Enable or configure RBAC rules with
least-privilege access to Secrets.

claims.rationale: Secret page: by default Secrets are stored unencrypted, and safe use requires encryption at rest and least-privilege RBAC. That is the additional access controls and storage protections the page refers to, and it follows that creating a Secret alone does not secure the data.

source.quote: create a namespace, deploy workloads, inspect resource ownership, break and repair an image rollout, tunnel traffic with `port-forward`, and remove the lab cleanly

additional_sources.quote: independently confirm a dedicated disposable cluster
rolling update settings, rollback behavior, and rollout progress
Start with an empty disposable namespace

claims.rationale: Module 1.2 exercise: deploy workloads, inspect them, repair an image rollout (an update) and clean up; module 1.4 requires a dedicated disposable cluster and covers rolling updates; module 1.6 practice runs in a disposable namespace. Together they cover deploying, inspecting, updating and cleaning up example workloads in a disposable cluster.

source.quote:
command: Specifies the operation that you want to perform on one or more resources,
for example create, get, describe, delete.

additional_sources.quote:
Kubernetes provides a command line tool for communicating with a Kubernetes cluster's
control plane,

claims.rationale: kubectl page: the tool communicates with the cluster and its commands create, get, describe and delete resources, i.e. interacting with and querying clusters. "Essential" is the module description's own framing of the basic command set; the page presents these as the core command operations and nothing contradicts it.

source.quote: Pods are the smallest deployable units of computing that you can create and manage in Kubernetes.

claims.rationale: Source defines Pods as the smallest deployable units that you create and manage in Kubernetes, covering both "smallest deployable" and "understanding and managing".

source.quote: Create a Deployment to rollout a ReplicaSet.

additional_sources.quote: DESIRED displays the desired number of replicas of the application, which you define when you create the Deployment. This is the desired state.

claims.rationale: Deployment page covers rollouts (create, update, rollback, pause) and the desired number of replicas that the controller maintains.

source.quote: Expose an application running in your cluster behind a single outward-facing endpoint, even when the workload is split across multiple backends.

additional_sources.quote: that Deployment can create and destroy Pods dynamically

forward traffic to one of the ready
endpoints associated with that Service

claims.rationale: Service page: one endpoint fronts multiple backend Pods, Pods are created and destroyed dynamically by a Deployment, and Service traffic is forwarded to one of the ready endpoints (distribution across backends). "Load balancing" is supported in this distribution sense; the page also says Kubernetes itself does not provide an external load-balancing component for type LoadBalancer, which the description does not claim.

source.quote: A ConfigMap is an API object used to store non-confidential data in key-value pairs.

additional_sources.quote: A ConfigMap allows you to decouple environment-specific configuration from your container images, so that your applications are easily portable.

A Secret is an object that contains a small amount of sensitive data such as
a password, a token, or a key.

claims.rationale: ConfigMap page: runtime configuration decoupled from images and consumed by Pods; Secret page: Secrets hold sensitive values. Matches "externalizing runtime configuration and handling sensitive values with Secrets".

source.quote:
Labels can be used to organize and to select subsets of
objects.

additional_sources.quote: namespaces provide a mechanism for isolating groups of resources within a single cluster

claims.rationale: Labels organize and select subsets of objects; namespaces isolate groups of resources in a cluster. Covers organizing, grouping and selecting resources within a cluster.

Required fields
